blocks.content: Picture a driving test. The examiner is not just checking if you know the rules of the road. They are watching how you actually drive in real traffic, with a real car, next to a real person.

A candidate who floors it without checking mirrors, freezes at an intersection, or ignores the examiner telling them to turn left is not failing because they do not know traffic rules. They are failing because of how they handled the drive.

System design interviews work the same way. Most candidates who get rejected are not rejected because they never heard of consistent hashing or database sharding. They are rejected because of a handful of repeatable, avoidable mistakes in how they handled the session.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529075-725290201.png
blocks.alt: Two paths, technical knowledge and judgment plus communication, both feeding into the hire signal

blocks.content: This topic is a checklist. It pulls together the failure patterns that show up again and again across real interview feedback, some of which we have already touched on elsewhere in this module, and puts them all in one place so you can run through them before your next interview.
1. Introduction
None of these mistakes are about missing knowledge. Every one of them is about behavior under pressure: what you say, what you stay quiet about, and how you spend your forty five minutes.

["Jumping straight into drawing boxes without clarifying requirements","Over engineering for imagined scale nobody asked for","Going silent when stuck instead of thinking out loud","Dropping buzzwords without being able to explain them one level deeper","Ignoring the interviewer's hints or redirections","Spending too long on one component and running out of time","Not asking about non functional requirements at all","Treating the interview as a monologue instead of a conversation"]
items: Jumping straight into drawing boxes without clarifying requirements
Over engineering for imagined scale nobody asked for
Going silent when stuck instead of thinking out loud
Dropping buzzwords without being able to explain them one level deeper
Ignoring the interviewer's hints or redirections
Spending too long on one component and running out of time
Not asking about non functional requirements at all
Treating the interview as a monologue instead of a conversation

blocks.title: Why this list matters
blocks.content: An interviewer forms most of their opinion about you in the first fifteen minutes and the last five. These mistakes cluster in exactly those windows, which is why fixing them moves your outcome more than memorizing another pattern does.
2. Mistake 1: Jumping straight into drawing boxes
blocks.text: 2. Mistake 1: Jumping straight into drawing boxes

blocks.content: The prompt lands, "design a ride sharing app," and within thirty seconds a candidate is already sketching a load balancer, an API gateway, and three microservices. It feels productive. It looks confident. It is usually the single most common reason a strong technical candidate still gets a weak rating.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529076-255004578.png
blocks.alt: Jumping to boxes leads to a design that guesses the wrong problem, clarifying first leads to a design matching the actual ask

blocks.content: The problem is not the boxes themselves, it is that nobody has agreed yet on what the system actually needs to do. Is this ride sharing app matching drivers in real time, or is it a scheduling tool for pre booked rides? Are we optimizing for a metro area or a whole country? None of that is obvious from one sentence, and guessing wrong means the rest of the interview is spent designing the wrong thing.

blocks.title: Already covered in depth
blocks.content: The full framework for asking good clarifying questions and stating assumptions lives in the requirement clarification topic in this module. This entry is here because it is genuinely the number one mistake, so it earns a place on this checklist too.
2.1 What works better instead

Spend the first three to five minutes only on questions. Who are the users, what is the core action they take, roughly how many of them are there, and what does success look like. Write the assumptions down where the interviewer can see them, then start drawing.
3. Mistake 2: Over engineering for imagined scale
blocks.text: 3. Mistake 2: Over engineering for imagined scale

blocks.content: The interviewer says this system needs to support ten thousand daily active users. The candidate hears that and, thirty minutes later, has drawn a design with Kafka event streams, geo sharded databases, and a multi region active active setup with automatic failover.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529076-202885007.png
blocks.alt: Interviewer states ten thousand users, candidate designs for one billion, adds Kafka sharding and multi region, interviewer reads this as poor judgment

blocks.content: This feels like showing off breadth of knowledge. It actually reads as the opposite. An interviewer watching this happen is not thinking "wow, this person knows a lot." They are thinking "this person cannot tell the difference between a problem that needs this complexity and one that does not."
3.1 Why it actually signals poor judgment
blocks.text: 3.1 Why it actually signals poor judgment

blocks.content: Every piece of infrastructure has an operational cost: more failure modes, more moving parts, more things to monitor and debug at three in the morning. Adding all of that for a scale nobody asked for tells the interviewer you would make the same call on the job, where it costs real engineering time and real money.
3.2 What works better instead

Design for the stated scale, then explicitly call out where the design would need to change if scale grew by ten times or a hundred times. That shows you understand the tradeoff axis without actually building the heavier system prematurely.

blocks.title: A useful gut check
blocks.content: If you are reaching for a piece of infrastructure and cannot say, in one sentence, which specific number from the requirements forced that choice, you are probably over engineering.
4. Mistake 3: Going silent when stuck

You hit a wall. Maybe you are not sure how to handle a race condition, maybe you forgot the exact tradeoff between two caching strategies. The instinct is to go quiet and think it through privately for a minute or two before speaking again.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529077-259392165.png
blocks.alt: Candidate goes quiet and the interviewer cannot follow the reasoning, candidate thinks out loud and the interviewer can track it

blocks.content: An interviewer cannot grade a silence. They cannot tell the difference between someone working through a hard problem and someone who is simply stuck with no path forward. Two minutes of silence in a forty five minute interview is a meaningful chunk of your evaluation window spent giving them nothing to score.
4.1 What works better instead

["\"I am weighing whether to use a queue here or a direct call, let me think through the tradeoff out loud\"","\"I am not fully sure how to solve this cleanly, here is what I am considering and why each option has a gap\"","\"Let me back up and check if I am even solving the right sub problem here\""]
items: "I am weighing whether to use a queue here or a direct call, let me think through the tradeoff out loud"
"I am not fully sure how to solve this cleanly, here is what I am considering and why each option has a gap"
"Let me back up and check if I am even solving the right sub problem here"

blocks.title: It is fine to be unsure
blocks.content: Verbalizing an incomplete or even a wrong train of thought is almost always scored better than silence, because it gives the interviewer something to react to and redirect if needed.
5. Mistake 4: Dropping buzzwords without understanding

"I would use CQRS here" or "we should use consistent hashing for this" can land well in the moment. The trouble starts the instant the interviewer asks the natural follow up: why does that apply here, and how does it actually work under the hood.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529077-599603523.png
blocks.alt: Candidate says CQRS, interviewer asks one follow up, either cannot explain further or explains the reasoning

blocks.content: Naming a pattern is not the same as understanding it. If consistent hashing comes up but you cannot explain what happens when a node is added or removed, or CQRS comes up but you cannot explain why splitting reads and writes actually solves your stated problem, the term becomes a liability instead of a strength.
5.1 What works better instead

Only introduce a term once you can defend it one level deeper. A simple test before you say it out loud: could you explain, in one sentence, the specific problem in this design that the term solves, and what would break without it. If you cannot answer that, describe the idea in plain language instead and let the interviewer supply the name if they want to.
6. Mistake 5: Ignoring the interviewer's hints

The interviewer asks, almost casually, "what happens if this endpoint gets hit a lot more than the others?" The candidate acknowledges it with a nod and keeps walking through their own planned outline, never actually answering the question.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529737-88098860.png
blocks.alt: Interviewer nudges toward caching, candidate either ignores it and misses the signal, or follows the nudge and shows adaptability

blocks.content: That question was not small talk. An interviewer nudging you toward a specific area, whether it is caching, a particular failure mode, or a part of the design you glossed over, is almost always a direct signal about what they want to see you reason through. Sticking rigidly to your own script instead of following that thread reads as inflexibility, not focus.
6.1 What works better instead

Treat any rephrased question, repeated question, or sudden change of topic from the interviewer as a flashing sign. Pause your outline, follow the thread they opened, and come back to your original plan afterward if there is time. This alone often separates a pass from a borderline outcome.
7. Mistake 6: Spending too long on one component
blocks.text: 7. Mistake 6: Spending too long on one component

blocks.content: Thirty minutes in, the candidate is still refining the exact columns and indexes of one database table. It is detailed, it is correct, and it is also a problem, because the interview is forty five minutes long and the overall architecture has not been discussed yet.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529739-910121318.png
blocks.alt: Thirty minutes spent on one schema leaves no time for architecture, and trade offs never get discussed

blocks.content: A beautifully normalized schema is worth very little if the interviewer never gets to ask about your API design, your caching layer, or how the system behaves during a partial outage. Depth on one component cannot substitute for breadth across the whole design.

{"headers":["Interview phase","Rough time budget"],"rows":[["Clarify requirements and scope","5 to 7 minutes"],["High level architecture","10 to 12 minutes"],["Deep dive on one or two components","15 to 18 minutes"],["Trade offs, failure modes, wrap up","8 to 10 minutes"]]}

blocks.title: Set a mental checkpoint
blocks.content: If you notice you have spent more than ten minutes on a single component without checking in with the interviewer, that is your cue to zoom back out.
8. Mistake 7: Not asking about non functional requirements at all
blocks.text: 8. Mistake 7: Not asking about non functional requirements at all

blocks.content: The entire interview goes by covering what the system does: users can post, users can follow, users can search. Latency, availability, consistency, and durability never come up once, not from the interviewer and not from the candidate.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529740-742714730.png
blocks.alt: Only features discussed means latency and availability never get asked, asking about NFRs early means the design reflects real constraints

blocks.content: Two systems with identical features can have completely different architectures depending on whether they need to respond in under one hundred milliseconds or a few seconds, whether they can tolerate occasional data loss, or whether every write needs to be immediately visible everywhere. Skipping this conversation means your design is not actually grounded in anything.
8.1 What works better instead

["Ask directly: what latency does this need to feel responsive to a user","Ask: can this tolerate brief unavailability, or does it need to stay up during a node failure","Ask: does every read need the absolute latest write, or is a short delay acceptable"]
items: Ask directly: what latency does this need to feel responsive to a user
Ask: can this tolerate brief unavailability, or does it need to stay up during a node failure
Ask: does every read need the absolute latest write, or is a short delay acceptable

blocks.content: 9. Mistake 8: Treating it as a monologue instead of a conversation
blocks.text: 9. Mistake 8: Treating it as a monologue instead of a conversation

blocks.content: Some candidates treat the forty five minutes like a rehearsed presentation: talk through the whole design start to finish, barely pausing, barely checking if the interviewer is following or agrees with the direction.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529740-79088957.png
blocks.alt: A monologue leads the interviewer to disengage, inviting input leads to collaborative problem solving

blocks.content: The strongest candidates treat this as two engineers solving a problem together at a whiteboard. They check in, they ask "does this direction make sense so far," and they genuinely adjust course based on the answer instead of treating it as a formality.
"Before I go further into the database layer, does this high level flow match what you had in mind, or is there a part you want me to dig into first?"
10. A worked example: same prompt, two answers
blocks.text: 10. A worked example: same prompt, two answers

blocks.content: Here is the same interview prompt handled two different ways, to make the difference concrete instead of abstract.
10.1 The prompt
"Design a system that lets users book appointments with service providers, like a salon or a clinic."
10.2 The weaker answer

blocks.title: Weaker answer
blocks.text: Sure, so we will have a microservices architecture with an API gateway, a booking service, a notification service, and a payments service. For scale we will use Kafka to handle events between services, and we will shard the database by provider ID so it can handle millions of bookings a day. I will also add consistent hashing for the caching layer.

blocks.title: What went wrong here
blocks.content: No clarifying questions were asked, so the scale, the region, and the actual booking flow are all guesses. Kafka, sharding, and consistent hashing are all named without being tied to any stated requirement, and the whole answer was delivered as one uninterrupted block with no check in.
10.3 The stronger answer

blocks.title: Stronger answer
blocks.text: Before I design anything, can I check a few things? Roughly how many providers and bookings a day are we expecting, and is double booking the same slot something we absolutely must prevent? ... Okay, so given a few thousand providers and double booking prevention is critical, I will start with a simple architecture: a booking service backed by a single relational database, since we need strong consistency on slot reservations. Does that match what you had in mind, or did you want to go deeper into how we prevent double booking specifically?

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529741-893982209.png
blocks.alt: Same prompt, weaker answer guesses and drops buzzwords in a monologue, stronger answer asks questions and reasons out loud in a conversation

blocks.title: What changed
blocks.content: The stronger answer asks before assuming, ties every design choice to a stated constraint, and explicitly hands the conversation back to the interviewer instead of running through a fixed script.
11. The interview angle

Every mistake on this list connects back to something else in this module. Clarifying requirements is its own topic because it is foundational, not just a nice to have. Capacity estimation exists so your scale decisions are grounded in numbers instead of guesses. Bottleneck identification and tradeoff justification are exactly the muscle you use instead of silently freezing or naming a buzzword you cannot defend.
None of these mistakes require new technical knowledge to fix. They require slowing down at the start, checking in throughout, and being honest in the moment about what you do and do not know.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396529741-100041141.png
blocks.alt: Clarify first, match the stated scale, think out loud, and ask about NFRs all feed into being ready for the next round

blocks.content: ["Clarify requirements before drawing anything","Design for the scale you were actually given","Think out loud instead of going quiet","Only use a term you can defend one level deeper","Follow the interviewer's hints, do not override them with your own script","Budget your time across the whole design, not just one component","Ask about latency, availability, and consistency needs explicitly","Run it as a conversation, checking in as you go"]
items: Clarify requirements before drawing anything
Design for the scale you were actually given
Think out loud instead of going quiet
Only use a term you can defend one level deeper
Follow the interviewer's hints, do not override them with your own script
Budget your time across the whole design, not just one component
Ask about latency, availability, and consistency needs explicitly
Run it as a conversation, checking in as you go

blocks.content: Fix these eight and the technical gaps that remain become much smaller problems to solve, because the interviewer is now actually able to see how you think.
